impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that Teva's anti-CGRP antibody headache patents were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112, after a jury had found willful infringement and no invalidity.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity for Teva's headache patents claiming methods of treating headache using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies. The court reinstated the jury's findings of willful infringement and validity, remanding the case. This is significant for the pharmaceutical industry as it addresses the scope of written description and enablement for antibody-based therapeutic claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with genus claims covering antibody therapeutics benefit from this ruling, as it supports broader patent protection where the specification discloses representative species and known methods of making the claimed class of antibodies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar competitors face increased risk that broad antibody patent claims will be upheld, potentially delaying market entry and increasing licensing costs.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that licenses exclusive commercialization rights but retains the right to independently sue for infringement has sufficient constitutional standing to bring a patent infringement action.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that a patent owner who retains the right to sue third parties for infringement retains a sufficient exclusionary right to satisfy Article III standing, even when it has granted an exclusive license for manufacturing and selling. This clarifies the standing framework for patent owners who structure licensing agreements while preserving enforcement rights.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners can structure license agreements to grant broad exclusive commercialization rights while retaining standing to enforce patents independently, providing flexibility in monetization and enforcement strategies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose the ability to challenge standing based on the argument that a patent owner transferred substantially all rights through an exclusive license when the licensor retained independent enforcement rights.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the statute of limitations had expired on Insulet's Defend Trade Secrets Act claim for misappropriation of insulin patch pump trade secrets before Insulet filed suit in 2023.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's denial of JMOL, holding that Insulet's DTSA claim was time-barred. The court found that Insulet knew or should have known of the misappropriation more than three years before filing suit in August 2023, given evidence that former employees shared trade secrets with EOFlow beginning in 2018. This decision vacated the jury's damages award and permanent injunction.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of trade secret misappropriation benefit from strict enforcement of the DTSA's three-year statute of limitations, particularly where the trade secret owner had early knowledge of employee departures and competitive product development.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners must act promptly upon learning of potential misappropriation; delay in filing suit risks losing the ability to recover damages even where misappropriation is proven at trial.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding Versata's trade secret damages expert and in overturning the jury's breach of contract damages award in a case involving Ford's alleged misappropriation of automotive configuration software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. The court also reversed the district court's override of the jury's breach of contract damages award, reinstating it. The court affirmed Ford's liability for trade secret misappropriation under both the DTSA and Michigan law. This case has significant implications for how courts evaluate damages methodologies in software trade secret cases.
impacts.positiveImplications: Trade secret plaintiffs benefit from the court's instruction that district courts should not too readily exclude damages models, particularly unjust enrichment theories, in software misappropriation cases. The reinstatement of the breach of contract jury award protects the role of juries in assessing contract damages.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop internal software while licensing third-party technology face heightened exposure to trade secret misappropriation claims and potentially larger damages awards on remand.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether sufficient evidence supported the jury's finding that four asserted trade secrets related to a cosmetic penile implant were protectable trade secrets under California law, and whether a related patent invalidity finding should also be reversed.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the denial of JMOL on trade secret claims, holding there was no legally sufficient evidence that the asserted trade secrets were protectable because the underlying ideas were generally known in the field. The court also reversed the patent invalidity finding, reasoning that if the ideas were generally known, they could not constitute an inventive contribution supporting co-inventorship. The permanent injunction and exemplary damages were vacated, though the counterfeiting claim and damages were affirmed.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants accused of trade secret misappropriation benefit from this holding, which reinforces that plaintiffs must prove with legally sufficient evidence that each asserted trade secret derives independent economic value from not being generally known.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret plaintiffs face a higher evidentiary bar to establish protectability, particularly where the asserted secrets overlap with knowledge generally known in the industry.

impacts.caseName: Enanta Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Pfizer Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a change from 'C2-C12-alkyl' in a provisional application to 'C1-C12-alkyl' in the non-provisional patent constituted correction of an obvious typographical error, thereby entitling the patent to the provisional's priority date and avoiding anticipation by Pfizer's public disclosure of nirmatrelvir.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity, holding that the alteration from C2 to C1 in the substituent definition was not an obvious typographical error and thus the patent could not claim priority from the provisional application. Because Pfizer's public disclosure of nirmatrelvir occurred between the provisional and non-provisional filing dates, the asserted claims were anticipated. This ruling invalidated Enanta's patent covering compounds related to Pfizer's Paxlovid COVID-19 treatment.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic and competing pharmaceutical companies benefit from strict application of priority date requirements, as errors in provisional applications that expand claim scope cannot be corrected through later filings without risking intervening prior art.
impacts.negativeImplications: Pharmaceutical patent holders face significant risk that even minor discrepancies between provisional and non-provisional applications can result in loss of priority date and patent invalidation, underscoring the critical importance of precision in provisional filings.

impacts.caseName: Ironburg Inventions Ltd. v. Valve Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly estopped Valve under 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(2) from asserting two invalidity grounds in litigation that were not raised in a prior IPR petition, based on the 'reasonably could have raised' standard.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's application of IPR estoppel against two invalidity grounds, finding insufficient evidence to support estoppel for one ground and that the district court failed to adequately account for hindsight bias in evaluating the other. The case was remanded for further proceedings. This decision narrows the scope of IPR estoppel under § 315(e)(2), giving accused infringers more latitude to raise invalidity defenses in district court litigation.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from a more rigorous standard for applying IPR estoppel, preserving their ability to raise invalidity defenses in district court that were not included in prior IPR petitions, particularly where prior art discovery was not straightforward.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face greater uncertainty about the preclusive effect of IPR proceedings, as defendants may more successfully argue that additional invalidity grounds should not be estopped.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming non-uniform constellations for digital communications are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the summary judgment of eligibility for claims of the '761 and '700 patents relating to non-uniform constellation designs, finding that further analysis under Alice was required. However, the court affirmed eligibility for claims of the '509 and '922 patents, affirmed the denial of JMOL on non-infringement, and affirmed the damages ruling including denial of the Daubert motion to exclude damages expert testimony. The case involves a significant willful infringement judgment in the communications technology space.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in the communications standards space benefit from the affirmation of eligibility for certain claims and the court's willingness to uphold jury verdicts on infringement and damages, including expert testimony on royalties.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies implementing industry standards face continued uncertainty about patent eligibility for mathematical optimization-based inventions, and the partial vacatur creates additional litigation costs on remand.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to automated systems for capturing, processing, and sharing farming data using GPS-equipped relay devices on farming equipment are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court erred in declining to find the case exceptional under § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that the asserted farming data collection patents are directed to patent-ineligible abstract ideas under § 101 but vacated and remanded the district court's determination that the case was not exceptional for purposes of attorney fee awards. The decision reinforces that using conventional computer hardware to automate data collection and processing in an agricultural context does not confer patent eligibility.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies accused of infringing agricultural data patents benefit from the confirmation that automating conventional data collection using standard hardware remains patent-ineligible, and the remand on exceptionality may enable fee recovery.
impacts.negativeImplications: AgTech patent holders face significant headwinds in enforcing patents that claim automated data collection and processing methods using conventional hardware, even in specialized farming contexts.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a jury verdict form that asked a single question on infringement covering all four asserted patents, without identifying which patent(s) were infringed, was prejudicial error requiring a new trial, and whether the district court erred on § 101 eligibility and non-infringement issues.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the infringement and damages judgments and remanded for a new trial, finding that the single-question verdict form covering all four asserted patents was deficient. The court also vacated and remanded for further proceedings on § 101 eligibility under Alice step two for one patent, while affirming eligibility for others and affirming the denial of JMOL on non-infringement. This decision emphasizes the importance of patent-specific verdict forms in multi-patent cases.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the requirement that verdict forms separately address infringement for each asserted patent, preventing ambiguous general verdicts that obscure the basis for liability.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent plaintiffs asserting multiple patents must ensure verdict forms allow patent-by-patent findings, and face the cost and risk of new trials when aggregate verdict forms are used.

impacts.caseName: Otsuka America Pharmaceutical, Inc. v. Hetero Labs Limited
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly construed the claim terms 'dextromethorphan' and 'quinidine' in a weight-to-weight ratio limitation to refer to the salt forms of these compounds, and whether the court erred in waiving the Rule 65(c) bond requirement for a preliminary injunction pending appeal.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's claim construction and preliminary injunction blocking Hetero's generic version of Nuedexta, but vacated the court's waiver of the bond requirement under Rule 65(c). The court held that the district court must require Otsuka to post a bond pending appeal to protect Hetero against potential damages from a wrongful injunction. This decision is significant for Hatch-Waxman litigation and the standards for preliminary injunctions in pharmaceutical patent cases.
impacts.positiveImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies benefit from the affirmation of the preliminary injunction blocking generic entry, reinforcing patent protection for combination drug products near patent expiration.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic pharmaceutical companies benefit from the requirement that a bond be posted even in strong patent cases, providing financial protection against wrongful injunctions that delay market entry.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTAB erred in its obviousness determination regarding sensor-based logistics patent claims, particularly the teaching of restricting access by reporting sensor information after a predetermined time delay.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's obviousness determination for FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent claims and remanded for further proceedings. The court declined to review the Board's denial of FedEx's motion to terminate the IPR on time-bar grounds under § 315(b), where Qualcomm filed its petition on the same day as the statutory deadline for the party sued in district court. This case raises important questions about third-party IPR petitions filed to circumvent the one-year time bar.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from the vacatur of the obviousness finding and the opportunity for reconsideration on remand, potentially preserving patent protection for sensor-based logistics technology.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent owners face continued risk from third-party IPR petitions that may be strategically timed to coincide with litigation deadlines, as the court declined to address the time-bar issue.

impacts.caseName: Actelion Pharmaceuticals Ltd v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' in an epoprostenol pharmaceutical composition patent refers to pH measured at the standard temperature of 25°C recognized in the field, and whether Actelion was barred from asserting infringement under the doctrine of equivalents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding of no infringement, holding that 'a pH of 13 or higher' is measured at the standard temperature of 25°C and that Actelion was barred from asserting infringement under the doctrine of equivalents. This decision is significant for pharmaceutical patent litigation because it establishes that pH values in patent claims are interpreted according to field-standard measurement conditions unless the specification indicates otherwise.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic pharmaceutical companies benefit from clear standards for interpreting scientifically measurable claim limitations, reducing uncertainty in ANDA litigation and supporting non-infringement defenses.
impacts.negativeImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies with patents using measurable scientific parameters face narrower claim scope when claims do not specify non-standard measurement conditions.

impacts.caseName: mCom IP, LLC v. City National Bank of Florida
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly dismissed a patent infringement complaint on obviousness grounds based on a prior IPR decision canceling related claims, and whether the court properly awarded attorney fees under § 285 and sanctions under § 1927.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the dismissal of mCom's patent infringement complaint for failure to state a claim, agreeing that the surviving patent claims were invalid on the same obviousness grounds applied to canceled claims in a prior IPR. However, the court reversed the § 285 exceptional case fee award and § 1927 attorney sanctions, finding insufficient grounds to conclude the case was exceptional or that counsel acted in bad faith. This decision sets an important limit on fee-shifting in patent cases where the complaint, while ultimately unsuccessful, was not frivolous.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent plaintiffs benefit from the reversal of fee-shifting, establishing that asserting surviving patent claims after partial IPR invalidation does not automatically make a case exceptional, protecting access to courts for patent enforcement.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers who successfully defend against weak patent claims may find it more difficult to recover attorney fees, even where the patent's remaining claims appear vulnerable based on prior IPR outcomes.

impacts.caseName: TrackTime, LLC v. Amazon.com Services LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claim terms reciting 'executable program code configured to' perform specified functions should be construed as means-plus-function limitations under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f), in light of the Federal Circuit's intervening decision in Dyfan, LLC v. Target Corp.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the district court's indefiniteness ruling for the '978 patent and remanded for reconsideration of whether § 112(f) applies to 'executable program code configured to' limitations, in light of the court's intervening Dyfan precedent. For the '638 patent, the court affirmed the jury's finding of anticipation invalidity. This decision provides important guidance on when software claim terms trigger means-plus-function treatment.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software patent holders benefit from the opportunity to argue that 'executable program code' limitations are not means-plus-function terms, potentially avoiding indefiniteness challenges that would invalidate their claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies defending against software patent claims face continued uncertainty about the scope of means-plus-function treatment for software claim terms until the district court resolves the issue on remand.
